title: Four ways to reach the CRM
scenario:
You are an operations manager at a property management company with 300 staff. The team wants its AI assistant to read and update tenant records in the company's CRM and to read files from the company's document store.

IT collected four options from different suppliers. The operations director asks you to recommend one for each need. The exhibit shows the shortlist.
exhibit:
Integration shortlist (made-up example data)

Need A: tenant records in the CRM (read and update)
  A1  Official remote MCP server, run by the CRM company
  A2  "ConnectAll": a start-up's server that passes requests to
      40 business apps, including our CRM
  A3  Reference server from GitHub, adapted by an intern

Need B: files in our document store (inside our network,
        not reachable from the internet)
  B1  The AI vendor's tunnel feature (status: research preview)
  B2  Copy all files to a public cloud folder each night

IT comment: "ConnectAll is listed in a public MCP directory,
so it is already security-checked."

questions.prompt: Which option for Need A fits OpenAI's MCP guide best?

options.text: A2, because one server for 40 apps means less work for IT in the future.
options.explanation: The guide calls such services aggregators and says to be extra careful with due diligence. It recommends the official server first.

options.text: A1, because the guide recommends official servers hosted by the service providers.
options.explanation: Right. The guide's example is the Stripe server hosted by Stripe, not one hosted by a third party.

options.text: A3, because code from the MCP project's GitHub is the most trusted source.
options.explanation: The servers repository README says reference servers are educational examples, not production-ready solutions.

options.text: Any of the three, because every MCP server works the same way and has the same risk.
options.explanation: They use the same protocol, but who runs the server decides who handles your data. The guide treats them differently.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the IT comment about ConnectAll?

options.text: Nothing: a public directory listing means the vendor has audited the server's security.
options.explanation: Anthropic's Claude Code security page says listing criteria are reviewed, but no MCP server is security-audited.

options.text: Directories list only official servers, so ConnectAll must be the CRM company's own server.
options.explanation: The exhibit says ConnectAll is a start-up's server. A listing doesn't make it official.

options.text: Directories are fine for internal tools, but never for servers that handle customer data.
options.explanation: The docs don't ban directory servers. They say a listing is not a security check, so you still review.

options.text: A listing is not a security check: vendors say they don't verify or audit third-party servers.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI says remote MCP servers are not verified by OpenAI, and Anthropic says it doesn't security-audit any MCP server.

questions.prompt: The intern's demo with A3 worked well. What should the director take from it?

options.text: It proves the idea, but reference servers are examples, not production-ready software.
options.explanation: Right. The repository's README says this and asks developers to add their own safeguards.

options.text: It is ready for production, because it comes from the official MCP project.
options.explanation: The README says the opposite: reference servers are educational examples, not production-ready.

options.text: It shows that A1 and A2 are not needed, because a free server does the same job.
options.explanation: A working demo doesn't mean safe, maintained software. Someone must own and secure it.

options.text: It shows the CRM's own server will fail, since the intern needed to adapt the code.
options.explanation: The demo says nothing about the CRM company's official server.

questions.prompt: For Need B, the AI vendor is Anthropic. What is the most accurate advice?

options.text: Choose B2: a public cloud folder is the only way an AI vendor can reach private files.
options.explanation: Both Anthropic and OpenAI document tunnels that reach private servers without exposing them to the internet.

options.text: Choose B1 and plan it as a critical, long-term service with guaranteed uptime from day one.
options.explanation: Anthropic's page says the tunnels are a research preview, provided as-is without uptime or support commitments.

options.text: B1 fits a pilot: it avoids exposing the files, but it is a research preview without uptime commitments.
options.explanation: Right. MCP tunnels use an outbound-only connection, and the page says they are a research preview that may change.

options.text: Neither: private files can never be connected to an AI assistant in any way.
options.explanation: The tunnel pages from both vendors describe how to connect private MCP servers.
